items.question: What is pattern matching in C#, and where does it appear?
items.answer: Pattern matching tests an expression for shape, type, or value and can introduce a variable when the test succeeds. The two expression forms are is and the switch expression. Switch statements also accept patterns. The vocabulary includes declaration and type, constant, relational, property, positional, list, var, discard, and the logical and, or, and not combinators. The compiler checks exhaustiveness on switch expressions and flags when an arm is already covered by an earlier one.

items.sixtySeconds: is and switch expressions. Match shape, bind a variable, compiler watches exhaustiveness.

items.question: When do you use a switch expression instead of if/else for auth providers?
items.answer: When the set of shapes is closed enough that missing a provider should be a compile-time or obvious runtime gap. Each arm returns a value. Learning Tools Interoperability (LTI) 1.3 versus an OpenID Connect (OIDC) bearer versus a legacy API key become property and list patterns, not nested ifs that forget a combination. Keep side effects out of arms; call named methods. The discard arm should throw with the unmatched value, not silently default to a privileged path.
followUps: How do you match on multiple properties of a token record?
What happens at runtime if no arm matches and you omitted _?
items.sixtySeconds: Closed set, one value per arm, throw on unknown. Property patterns for LTI versus OIDC versus API key.

items.question: How does with relate to immutability?
items.answer: Records are reference types (or record structs) with value-based equality and a compiler-generated copy constructor. with allocates a copy and sets the listed properties. Concurrent attempt-submit code can snapshot a scoring policy record and pass the copy into a worker without a lock around field writes. with does not deep-copy nested mutable lists; those still need their own immutability story.
followUps: Does with work on ordinary classes?
What is init versus set on the copied properties?
items.sixtySeconds: with copies a record. Original unchanged. Nested mutable collections are still shared.

items.question: Name four pattern kinds and one production use each.
items.answer: Declaration and type: if (seq is IList<T> list) for O(1) count. Relational: score bands on an attempt. Property: auth provider records. List: ragged CSV import rows with [_, kind, .., amount]. Logical not: is not null. Positional: Deconstruct on a record in a switch arm.
followUps: What does .. mean in a list pattern?
Can you use patterns in an is expression outside switch?
items.sixtySeconds: Type, property, relational, list. CSV rows and auth records are the stories to tell.

items.question: How does C# exhaustiveness differ from TypeScript discriminated unions?
items.answer: On a closed enum or record hierarchy, Roslyn emits CS8509 when a switch expression arm is missing. TypeScript uses a never check in default for union exhaustiveness — erased at runtime. C# enums from wire data are not closed — any int casts to the enum — so you need _ => throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException. TypeScript discriminated unions narrow on a kind field; C# sealed record hierarchy plus switch is the runtime-preserved equivalent.
items.sixtySeconds: Closed enum compiler enforced. Wire int needs discard throw. Record hierarchy equals TS union. never equals discard throw.

items.question: Design auth token handling as discriminated unions in C#.
items.answer: Use sealed records: LtiToken, OidcBearer, ApiKeyToken inheriting from AuthToken. Switch on token returns AuthDecision per arm. Use when guards for version prefixes like LTI 1.3 versus 1.3.0. Discard throws UnauthorizedAccessException — never guest default. with snapshots role changes under concurrency. Integration tests feed every wire shape plus one garbage payload.

items.sixtySeconds: Sealed records per provider. Switch narrows. when for versions. Discard throws. with for roles.

items.question: When is an expression-bodied member not a lambda?
items.answer: => on a method or property is shorthand for a single-expression body — it compiles to a normal IL method, not a delegate unless you pass it as one. Local functions cannot be declared inside expression-bodied members. Use a block body when you need locals, multiple statements, or clear await sequencing. Pairing => methods with switch expressions is idiomatic for small policy helpers.
followUps: Arrow fields on JS classes versus => members?
items.sixtySeconds: => member is body sugar not lambda. Block for multi-step. switch in => is fine. No local functions inside.

items.question: How do list patterns help on a ragged CSV import?
items.answer: Match [_, "SKU", .., var price] on a string array or split row — fails to the next arm if shape does not fit. Combine with when decimal.TryParse(price, out _). This is compile-checked shape matching, not JavaScript destructuring that yields undefined. Requires a countable indexer sequence, not bare IEnumerable. Reject bad rows before allocating domain objects.
followUps: What happens if var catch-all is first?
items.sixtySeconds: List plus .. for ragged CSV. and not &&. Indexer sequence required. Catch-all last.

items.question: A concurrent worker mutates Roles on a shared AuthDecision — what is the fix?
items.answer: with creates a shallow snapshot — top-level fields copied, nested List still shared. Fix: snapshot with with and replace Roles with an immutable copy: live with { Roles = live.Roles.Append(role).ToImmutableArray() }. Never mutate a list on a record that other threads still reference. Same shallow-copy trap as JavaScript object spread.
followUps: record struct with for hot paths?
items.sixtySeconds: with shallow. Replace nested list in with. ImmutableArray for roles. No shared mutable list.
